explain.say: Electricity crosses the country on pylons at very high voltage, up to 400,000 volts in Britain, because that cuts the energy wasted in the wires. A substation is where the voltage is changed and the power is shared out.

explain.say: Power first passes huge circuit breakers. If lightning strikes or a line is damaged, they open in a fraction of a second to cut off the faulty part and protect everything else.

explain.say: Transformers then step the voltage down. Coils of wire around an iron core turn high-voltage, low-current power into lower-voltage, higher-current power that local cables can carry.

explain.say: Thick metal busbars share the power between outgoing circuits at around 11,000 volts. Small transformers in streets, often in green boxes, then lower it again to about 230 volts for homes.

faq.q: Why does electricity travel at such high voltage?
faq.a: For the same power, a higher voltage needs a smaller current, and the heat lost in a wire depends on the current squared. So stepping up to hundreds of thousands of volts makes long-distance losses small.
asks: Why are pylon voltages so high?

faq.q: What do circuit breakers in a substation do?
faq.a: They are giant automatic switches. When sensors detect a fault, like a fallen line, they open within a fraction of a second, quenching the spark with special gas or a vacuum, to isolate the fault.
asks: How does a substation protect the grid?

faq.q: How does a substation lower the voltage?
faq.a: A transformer has two coils wrapped round an iron core. Alternating current in the first coil makes a changing magnetic field, which drives current in the second coil; with fewer turns on the second coil, the voltage is lower.
asks: How does a step-down transformer work?

faq.q: What is the green box in my street?
faq.a: It is usually a small local substation or transformer that lowers the voltage from about 11,000 volts to the 230 volts used in homes. It may hum gently, which is the transformer core vibrating.
Transformer cores stretch and shrink very slightly every time the magnetic field changes, 100 times a second on a 50 hertz grid, which makes a low hum.
asks: What is the buzzing noise from a substation?

facts: Britain's main transmission network runs at 400,000 and 275,000 volts, with 132,000 volts also used in Scotland.
Homes in Britain receive electricity at about 230 volts.
